bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Competition from dumped/low-priced Chinese solar glass and duty circumvention through third countries — China accounts for over 96% of total global solar glass capacity. Following anti-dumping duties on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam in December 2024, import patterns shifted rather than stopped — production has increasingly moved to Malaysia and Indonesia, which are not currently subject to such duties. Management also flags trans-shipment through Southeast Asian hubs and inventory dumping as practices that may undermine trade protections, distort pricing and disrupt fair competition, and the possibility that Chinese manufacturers set up production facilities in other countries to access key markets like India.
- Dependence on policy and trade-remedy support; adverse shifts in incentives or compliance requirements — Management states that policy and regulatory developments remain critical, as shifts in incentives or compliance requirements may directly influence pricing, project economics and profitability. Structural support currently comes from ALMM, Basic Customs Duties and the anti-dumping/countervailing duties the Company championed; timely policy intervention is repeatedly cited as necessary to safeguard domestic manufacturers, including against surplus Chinese capacity being redirected to India during prolonged US-China tariff tensions.
- Emergence of integrated module players with captive solar glass capacity — Within the solar glass sector, the emergence of integrated players with captive capacities creates the risk of sporadic supply of surplus production entering the open market, triggering price-based competition and margin pressures. Management separately notes that as large players increasingly shift toward captive consumption, surplus capacities are driving pricing pressures alongside aggressive tariff bidding.
- Missing upstream domestic value chain (polysilicon, ingots, wafers) exposing the sector to input supply and pricing shocks — Capacity in upstream segments such as polysilicon, ingots and wafers remains non-existent in India and continues to evolve; any gaps in these critical inputs could expose the sector to supply chain disruptions and pricing pressures, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Management expects ingot and wafer exposure to ease over the next 2-3 years as new capacities are set up, but states the threat still continues in the case of polysilicon — relevant because ALMM List-III will require domestic wafers and ingots by 2028.
- Single-product, single-segment concentration in flat (solar) glass — The Company's operations are focused on a single primary business segment, the manufacture of flat glass, with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is disclosed only on a geographical basis. Earnings therefore track one product's pricing cycle, which is the same cycle exposed to import dumping and captive-capacity surplus.
- Weak European module manufacturing base undermining the Company's European operations — In Europe, policy implementation gaps have led to the closure of several module manufacturing facilities as cheap imports of solar modules flood the markets, weakening competitiveness. This is a direct demand risk for the Company's European furnace, and Europe/Turkey lead its exports. In the United States, trade tensions intensified in April 2026 with triple-digit anti-dumping duties (123.04%) on solar imports from India and Southeast Asian hubs.
- Geopolitical instability in the Middle East disrupting fuel and freight — Geopolitical risks in the Middle East cause supply chain issues for critical inputs like oil & gas, raise commodity prices, increase freight costs and delay critical component deliveries. Disruptions to critical fuel supply routes have caused problems including escalating prices — material for an energy-intensive furnace operator.
- Cyber security and data privacy exposure — Identified in the BRSR material issues table as a negative-implication risk: any compromise of customer privacy or data security may result in reputational harm, missed business opportunities and increased legal exposure; cybersecurity incidents can interrupt operations, expose sensitive information and lead to financial losses from litigation, regulatory penalties and remediation costs. Cyber Security is among the top enterprise-level risks reviewed by the Board's Risk Management Committee.

outlook.body:
- Pivot to India: deconsolidate the European operations (wholly owned subsidiary Geosphere Glassworks and step-down subsidiary Glasmanufaktur Brandenburg, both in insolvency) to stem recurring losses and free management bandwidth and capital for deployment in India.
- Scale domestic capacity while maintaining financial discipline - the Bharuch expansion, enhanced to 600 TPD, takes combined installed capacity to 1,600 TPD (~10.5 GW of annual solar module demand).
- Differentiate through product innovation: 2 mm fully tempered solar glass as the flagship offering aligned to the industry's shift to bifacial and glass-glass modules, plus high-performance anti-reflective and anti-soiling coatings, antimony-free NoSbEra, antiglare Selene, matt-finish Shakti, BIPV rooftop and greenhouse glass, and grid-printed back glass for bifacial modules.
- Enter the rooftop solar segment as a new vertical, offering Borosil-branded solar panels along with inverters and lithium battery storage to provide end-to-end rooftop solutions, through a dual-channel go-to-market: a direct-to-customer model (installation via approved system integrators) and a distribution model (distributors installing through approved system integrators).
- Maintain multi-fuel furnace firing capability, the prior investment that allowed operations to continue without disruption through West Asia conflict-driven natural gas/LPG shortages and supplier force majeure declarations.
- Raise the share of green energy in manufacturing and reduce power cost/price volatility through captive wind-solar hybrid power under a group captive mechanism.
- Fund growth from equity while maintaining balance sheet prudence - preferential issues of equity shares and warrants broadened the investor base to support the expansion; the Board recommended no dividend in order to conserve resources for future growth.
- Sustain high-capacity utilisation and tight control over input costs; intensify efficiency and cost-cutting efforts in response to the fuel cost shock.
- Pursue export opportunities as the USA restricts import of glass from companies of Chinese origin, while continuing to serve both domestic and international markets from the 100-acre Bharuch, Gujarat facility.
- Strengthen quality through the in-house R&D function, aligning systems with evolving global standards.
- Advance responsible resource management and community engagement - groundwater recharge wells and CSR programmes in healthcare, education, horticulture and environmental stewardship.

outlook.body: Borosil Renewables' expansion is concentrated at its single flagship solar-glass complex at Bharuch, Gujarat, a 100-acre site described as India's first and largest solar glass facility. The company's capacity has been built in steps: India's first solar glass line of 180 TPD in 2010, expansion to 450 TPD (equivalent to 2.8 GW/annum) in 2019, and a further 550 TPD addition in 2023 taking India capacity to a total of 1,000 TPD (equivalent to 6.5 GW per annum). The AR's combined-installed-capacity chart traces the same path across furnaces - Furnace 1 (India) 240 TPD, Furnace 2 (India) 210 TPD, Furnace 3 (India) 550 TPD, plus Furnace 1 (Europe) - from 180 TPD in CY18 to 1,000 TPD at July CY25, with 1,600 TPD shown as the Est CY26 position. The live project is the 600 TPD expansion designated SG 4&5, on which work was commenced during 2025. The company states the 600 TPD project entails an investment of Rs 950 crores and is targeted for completion by December 2026; once operational, total installed capacity will increase to 1,600 TPD, enabling it to support approximately 10.5 GW of solar module demand annually - described in the report as 'Combined Solar Glass Capacity Planned: 1600 TPD (~10.5 GW)'. The expansion is funded from a 2025 preferential issue of equity shares and warrants raising Rs 517.66 crores plus an additional Rs 371.49 crores, explicitly earmarked to expand production capacity by 60% at the Bharuch facility. Alongside glass capacity, the company invested in a second captive power plant of 16.5 MW of wind-solar hybrid generation under a group captive mechanism with high plant load factor; this plant achieved commercial operations in March 2026 (against an expectation of September 2025) and allows the company to meet about 75% of its power requirement from green energy while reducing power cost. On the product-mix side, the share of 2 mm glass production was raised to 75% with the stated aim of reaching 100% by Q4 FY 2026-27, and grid-printed glasses for bifacial modules were successfully introduced. Product/application widening also continues into greenhouse glass, anti-glare glass and Building-Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV). Working against this domestic build-out, the European footprint has been exited rather than expanded: step-down subsidiary GMB Glasmanufaktur Brandenburg GmbH discontinued production and filed for insolvency on July 04, 2025, and its holding company Geosphere Glassworks GmbH filed for insolvency on December 22, 2025, with the Board writing off the Rs 32,590.81 lakhs exposure; the Europe furnace consequently drops out of the combined capacity chart. Demand-side context cited for the expansion is India adding a record ~44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26 and cumulative solar installed capacity crossing 150 GW (150.26 GW as of March 31, 2026), against domestic solar glass production currently estimated at around 18 GW and expected to increase sharply to nearly 51 GW by FY 2026-27 as new capacities by existing and new entrants commence operations.

outlook.body:
- India added a record 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26, nearly double the 23.8 GW added in the previous fiscal, and crossed the 150 GW milestone, reaching 150.26 GW installed as of March 31, 2026; with a target of 280 GW by 2030 the trajectory reflects strong forward demand across the solar value chain.
- Anti-dumping duty on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam, effective December 04, 2024 and valid till December 03, 2029, drove the increase in domestic selling prices from January 2025 - the main reason for the revenue and EBITDA improvement, in a market that was otherwise battling for survival after the earlier duty lapsed in August 2022.
- Average ex-factory selling price realised rose to `146.7/mm from `113.4/mm, contributing significantly to the turnaround in revenue and EBITDA margin; the Chairman describes pricing as having stabilised in the `147/mm range with EBITDA margins rebounding to 32%.
- Revenue/EBITDA improvement also came from a 6% increase in production and stock reduction, on high-capacity utilisation and tight input cost control.
- Management is confident of maintaining the January/March 2026 quarter performance, barring unforeseen circumstances.
- Domestic solar glass production, currently estimated at around 18 GW, is expected to increase sharply to nearly 51 GW by FY 2026-27 as new capacities by existing and new entrants commence operations, substantially substituting imports.
- Domestic module manufacturing capacity reached approximately 193 GW as of May 01, 2026, supported by ALMM and the PLI scheme; solar cell capacity under ALMM List-II reached 30 GW with capacities under installation expected to raise this to nearly 75 GW by 2027, and announced additions could surpass 100 GW over the medium term - supporting annual solar installations of nearly 75 GW on a DC basis.
- ALMM List-III has been announced from June 2028, under which domestically produced ingots and wafers become mandatory; leading module and cell manufacturers have announced upstream integration with aggregate ingot and wafer capacity expected to reach approximately 50-60 GW.
- Capacity additions among key customers and preparedness for upcoming demand strengthen the Company's domestic market standing, alongside a dependable supply base and faster turnaround times versus new entrants.
- C&I has emerged as a big growth area, helping industries reduce the cost of power and become more competitive, alongside a balanced mix of utility-scale solar parks, decentralised rooftop installations and agriculture water pumps.
- The India-EU Free Trade Agreement concluded on January 27, 2026 gives India preferential access to European markets, where solar demand is expected to remain steady at approximately 65-67 GW annually through 2030, positioning India as a strategic supplier.
- Global PV module prices are recovering from the historic lows of late 2024 following China's withdrawal of VAT export rebates effective April 01, 2026 and voluntary production cuts by major manufacturers, though trade barriers have intensified procurement challenges in the US and Europe.
- EU solar installations contracted marginally by 0.7% in 2025 to 65.1 GW from 65.6 GW in 2024, and the Company's major export markets continue to face low demand; exports were 7.38% of turnover versus 7.85% last year.
- Fuel prices of imported gas used by most industries more than doubled and furnace oil prices rose by almost 50% on the West Asia war; the Company requested customers to accept a fuel surcharge covering part of the cost increase, did not curtail production and maintained full production, and states the rise in fuel cost has not impacted margins.
- GMB's revenue collapse is attributed to discontinuation of production in view of the sharp drop in demand after solar module manufacturing capacity shut down in the EU.
- The Company operates in a single primary business segment - the manufacture of flat glass - with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is presented only by geography (within India / outside India).
- Macro backdrop: IMF projects global growth of 3.1% in CY 2026 and 3.0% in CY 2027 with global inflation rising modestly to 4.4% in CY 2026; India's economy is estimated to have grown 7.6% in FY 2025-26, with Union Budget 2026-27 prioritising scaling manufacturing and deepening domestic value chains.

deepdive.thesis: A strong, price-and-protection-driven quarter: standalone sales +53% YoY to Rs 405.69 cr with EBITDA at 35% (Rs 142 cr) — a 4th straight quarter above 33% — as anti-dumping/CVD walls (China/Vietnam ADD since Dec-24; Malaysia CVD 9.71% extended 5 yrs) plus a domestic supply gap (local solar glass meets only ~25% of demand) hold import-parity pricing, while a fuel surcharge (Rs 9.50/sqm from 10-Mar-26) offsets the West-Asia-war energy spike. Plants ran at full 1,000 TPD; a new solar-wind hybrid captive lifted renewable power to 93% (~Rs 18 cr/yr savings). The core catalyst is the **600 TPD expansion (1,000→1,600 TPD, +60%)** — construction done by Dec-26, both furnaces (SG4/SG5) commissioned by Mar-27, revenue from FY28, adding ~Rs 80-85 cr incremental EBITDA/quarter. Management aspires to grow from ~Rs 2,500 cr to Rs 4,000 cr+ in 3-4 years and is deciding the next furnace/adjacency within ~6 months. Note the reported PAT optics: Q4FY26's Rs 169 cr carried a Rs 75 cr one-off tax write-back (German write-off), so the QoQ "profit halving" to ~Rs 87 cr is an artifact, not operational decay.

risks.note: China accounts for over 96% of total global solar glass capacity. Following anti-dumping duties on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam in December 2024, import patterns shifted rather than stopped — production has increasingly moved to Malaysia and Indonesia, which are not currently subject to such duties. Management also flags trans-shipment through Southeast Asian hubs and inventory dumping as practices that may undermine trade protections, distort pricing and disrupt fair competition, and the possibility that Chinese manufacturers set up production facilities in other countries to access key markets like India.
risks.risk: Competition from dumped/low-priced Chinese solar glass and duty circumvention through third countries

risks.note: Management states that policy and regulatory developments remain critical, as shifts in incentives or compliance requirements may directly influence pricing, project economics and profitability. Structural support currently comes from ALMM, Basic Customs Duties and the anti-dumping/countervailing duties the Company championed; timely policy intervention is repeatedly cited as necessary to safeguard domestic manufacturers, including against surplus Chinese capacity being redirected to India during prolonged US-China tariff tensions.
risks.risk: Dependence on policy and trade-remedy support; adverse shifts in incentives or compliance requirements

risks.note: Within the solar glass sector, the emergence of integrated players with captive capacities creates the risk of sporadic supply of surplus production entering the open market, triggering price-based competition and margin pressures. Management separately notes that as large players increasingly shift toward captive consumption, surplus capacities are driving pricing pressures alongside aggressive tariff bidding.
risks.risk: Emergence of integrated module players with captive solar glass capacity

risks.note: Capacity in upstream segments such as polysilicon, ingots and wafers remains non-existent in India and continues to evolve; any gaps in these critical inputs could expose the sector to supply chain disruptions and pricing pressures, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Management expects ingot and wafer exposure to ease over the next 2-3 years as new capacities are set up, but states the threat still continues in the case of polysilicon — relevant because ALMM List-III will require domestic wafers and ingots by 2028.
risks.risk: Missing upstream domestic value chain (polysilicon, ingots, wafers) exposing the sector to input supply and pricing shocks

risks.note: The Company's operations are focused on a single primary business segment, the manufacture of flat glass, with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is disclosed only on a geographical basis. Earnings therefore track one product's pricing cycle, which is the same cycle exposed to import dumping and captive-capacity surplus.
risks.risk: Single-product, single-segment concentration in flat (solar) glass

risks.note: In Europe, policy implementation gaps have led to the closure of several module manufacturing facilities as cheap imports of solar modules flood the markets, weakening competitiveness. This is a direct demand risk for the Company's European furnace, and Europe/Turkey lead its exports. In the United States, trade tensions intensified in April 2026 with triple-digit anti-dumping duties (123.04%) on solar imports from India and Southeast Asian hubs.
risks.risk: Weak European module manufacturing base undermining the Company's European operations

risks.note: Geopolitical risks in the Middle East cause supply chain issues for critical inputs like oil & gas, raise commodity prices, increase freight costs and delay critical component deliveries. Disruptions to critical fuel supply routes have caused problems including escalating prices — material for an energy-intensive furnace operator.
risks.risk: Geopolitical instability in the Middle East disrupting fuel and freight

currentContext.expansion: Borosil Renewables' expansion is concentrated at its single flagship solar-glass complex at Bharuch, Gujarat, a 100-acre site described as India's first and largest solar glass facility. The company's capacity has been built in steps: India's first solar glass line of 180 TPD in 2010, expansion to 450 TPD (equivalent to 2.8 GW/annum) in 2019, and a further 550 TPD addition in 2023 taking India capacity to a total of 1,000 TPD (equivalent to 6.5 GW per annum). The AR's combined-installed-capacity chart traces the same path across furnaces - Furnace 1 (India) 240 TPD, Furnace 2 (India) 210 TPD, Furnace 3 (India) 550 TPD, plus Furnace 1 (Europe) - from 180 TPD in CY18 to 1,000 TPD at July CY25, with 1,600 TPD shown as the Est CY26 position. The live project is the 600 TPD expansion designated SG 4&5, on which work was commenced during 2025. The company states the 600 TPD project entails an investment of Rs 950 crores and is targeted for completion by December 2026; once operational, total installed capacity will increase to 1,600 TPD, enabling it to support approximately 10.5 GW of solar module demand annually - described in the report as 'Combined Solar Glass Capacity Planned: 1600 TPD (~10.5 GW)'. The expansion is funded from a 2025 preferential issue of equity shares and warrants raising Rs 517.66 crores plus an additional Rs 371.49 crores, explicitly earmarked to expand production capacity by 60% at the Bharuch facility. Alongside glass capacity, the company invested in a second captive power plant of 16.5 MW of wind-solar hybrid generation under a group captive mechanism with high plant load factor; this plant achieved commercial operations in March 2026 (against an expectation of September 2025) and allows the company to meet about 75% of its power requirement from green energy while reducing power cost. On the product-mix side, the share of 2 mm glass production was raised to 75% with the stated aim of reaching 100% by Q4 FY 2026-27, and grid-printed glasses for bifacial modules were successfully introduced. Product/application widening also continues into greenhouse glass, anti-glare glass and Building-Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV). Working against this domestic build-out, the European footprint has been exited rather than expanded: step-down subsidiary GMB Glasmanufaktur Brandenburg GmbH discontinued production and filed for insolvency on July 04, 2025, and its holding company Geosphere Glassworks GmbH filed for insolvency on December 22, 2025, with the Board writing off the Rs 32,590.81 lakhs exposure; the Europe furnace consequently drops out of the combined capacity chart. Demand-side context cited for the expansion is India adding a record ~44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26 and cumulative solar installed capacity crossing 150 GW (150.26 GW as of March 31, 2026), against domestic solar glass production currently estimated at around 18 GW and expected to increase sharply to nearly 51 GW by FY 2026-27 as new capacities by existing and new entrants commence operations.

risks.risk: Competition from dumped/low-priced Chinese solar glass and duty circumvention through third countries
risks.note: China accounts for over 96% of total global solar glass capacity. Following anti-dumping duties on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam in December 2024, import patterns shifted rather than stopped — production has increasingly moved to Malaysia and Indonesia, which are not currently subject to such duties. Management also flags trans-shipment through Southeast Asian hubs and inventory dumping as practices that may undermine trade protections, distort pricing and disrupt fair competition, and the possibility that Chinese manufacturers set up production facilities in other countries to access key markets like India.

risks.risk: Dependence on policy and trade-remedy support; adverse shifts in incentives or compliance requirements
risks.note: Management states that policy and regulatory developments remain critical, as shifts in incentives or compliance requirements may directly influence pricing, project economics and profitability. Structural support currently comes from ALMM, Basic Customs Duties and the anti-dumping/countervailing duties the Company championed; timely policy intervention is repeatedly cited as necessary to safeguard domestic manufacturers, including against surplus Chinese capacity being redirected to India during prolonged US-China tariff tensions.

risks.risk: Emergence of integrated module players with captive solar glass capacity
risks.note: Within the solar glass sector, the emergence of integrated players with captive capacities creates the risk of sporadic supply of surplus production entering the open market, triggering price-based competition and margin pressures. Management separately notes that as large players increasingly shift toward captive consumption, surplus capacities are driving pricing pressures alongside aggressive tariff bidding.

risks.risk: Missing upstream domestic value chain (polysilicon, ingots, wafers) exposing the sector to input supply and pricing shocks
risks.note: Capacity in upstream segments such as polysilicon, ingots and wafers remains non-existent in India and continues to evolve; any gaps in these critical inputs could expose the sector to supply chain disruptions and pricing pressures, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Management expects ingot and wafer exposure to ease over the next 2-3 years as new capacities are set up, but states the threat still continues in the case of polysilicon — relevant because ALMM List-III will require domestic wafers and ingots by 2028.

risks.risk: Single-product, single-segment concentration in flat (solar) glass
risks.note: The Company's operations are focused on a single primary business segment, the manufacture of flat glass, with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is disclosed only on a geographical basis. Earnings therefore track one product's pricing cycle, which is the same cycle exposed to import dumping and captive-capacity surplus.

risks.risk: Weak European module manufacturing base undermining the Company's European operations
risks.note: In Europe, policy implementation gaps have led to the closure of several module manufacturing facilities as cheap imports of solar modules flood the markets, weakening competitiveness. This is a direct demand risk for the Company's European furnace, and Europe/Turkey lead its exports. In the United States, trade tensions intensified in April 2026 with triple-digit anti-dumping duties (123.04%) on solar imports from India and Southeast Asian hubs.

risks.risk: Geopolitical instability in the Middle East disrupting fuel and freight
risks.note: Geopolitical risks in the Middle East cause supply chain issues for critical inputs like oil & gas, raise commodity prices, increase freight costs and delay critical component deliveries. Disruptions to critical fuel supply routes have caused problems including escalating prices — material for an energy-intensive furnace operator.

risks.risk: Cyber security and data privacy exposure
risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material issues table as a negative-implication risk: any compromise of customer privacy or data security may result in reputational harm, missed business opportunities and increased legal exposure; cybersecurity incidents can interrupt operations, expose sensitive information and lead to financial losses from litigation, regulatory penalties and remediation costs. Cyber Security is among the top enterprise-level risks reviewed by the Board's Risk Management Committee.

one-line thesis: A strong, price-and-protection-driven quarter: standalone sales +53% YoY to Rs 405.69 cr with EBITDA at 35% (Rs 142 cr) — a 4th straight quarter above 33% — as anti-dumping/CVD walls (China/Vietnam ADD since Dec-24; Malaysia CVD 9.71% extended 5 yrs) plus a domestic supply gap (local solar glass meets only ~25% of demand) hold import-parity pricing, while a fuel surcharge (Rs 9.50/sqm from 10-Mar-26) offsets the West-Asia-war energy spike. Plants ran at full 1,000 TPD; a new solar-wind hybrid captive lifted renewable power to 93% (~Rs 18 cr/yr savings). The core catalyst is the **600 TPD expansion (1,000→1,600 TPD, +60%)** — construction done by Dec-26, both furnaces (SG4/SG5) commissioned by Mar-27, revenue from FY28, adding ~Rs 80-85 cr incremental EBITDA/quarter. Management aspires to grow from ~Rs 2,500 cr to Rs 4,000 cr+ in 3-4 years and is deciding the next furnace/adjacency within ~6 months. Note the reported PAT optics: Q4FY26's Rs 169 cr carried a Rs 75 cr one-off tax write-back (German write-off), so the QoQ "profit halving" to ~Rs 87 cr is an artifact, not operational decay.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India added a record 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26, nearly double the 23.8 GW added in the previous fiscal, and crossed the 150 GW milestone, reaching 150.26 GW installed as of March 31, 2026; with a target of 280 GW by 2030 the trajectory reflects strong forward demand across the solar value chain.
- Anti-dumping duty on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam, effective December 04, 2024 and valid till December 03, 2029, drove the increase in domestic selling prices from January 2025 - the main reason for the revenue and EBITDA improvement, in a market that was otherwise battling for survival after the earlier duty lapsed in August 2022.
- Average ex-factory selling price realised rose to `146.7/mm from `113.4/mm, contributing significantly to the turnaround in revenue and EBITDA margin; the Chairman describes pricing as having stabilised in the `147/mm range with EBITDA margins rebounding to 32%.
- Revenue/EBITDA improvement also came from a 6% increase in production and stock reduction, on high-capacity utilisation and tight input cost control.
- Management is confident of maintaining the January/March 2026 quarter performance, barring unforeseen circumstances.
- Domestic solar glass production, currently estimated at around 18 GW, is expected to increase sharply to nearly 51 GW by FY 2026-27 as new capacities by existing and new entrants commence operations, substantially substituting imports.
- Domestic module manufacturing capacity reached approximately 193 GW as of May 01, 2026, supported by ALMM and the PLI scheme; solar cell capacity under ALMM List-II reached 30 GW with capacities under installation expected to raise this to nearly 75 GW by 2027, and announced additions could surpass 100 GW over the medium term - supporting annual solar installations of nearly 75 GW on a DC basis.
- ALMM List-III has been announced from June 2028, under which domestically produced ingots and wafers become mandatory; leading module and cell manufacturers have announced upstream integration with aggregate ingot and wafer capacity expected to reach approximately 50-60 GW.
- Capacity additions among key customers and preparedness for upcoming demand strengthen the Company's domestic market standing, alongside a dependable supply base and faster turnaround times versus new entrants.
- C&I has emerged as a big growth area, helping industries reduce the cost of power and become more competitive, alongside a balanced mix of utility-scale solar parks, decentralised rooftop installations and agriculture water pumps.
- The India-EU Free Trade Agreement concluded on January 27, 2026 gives India preferential access to European markets, where solar demand is expected to remain steady at approximately 65-67 GW annually through 2030, positioning India as a strategic supplier.
- Global PV module prices are recovering from the historic lows of late 2024 following China's withdrawal of VAT export rebates effective April 01, 2026 and voluntary production cuts by major manufacturers, though trade barriers have intensified procurement challenges in the US and Europe.
- EU solar installations contracted marginally by 0.7% in 2025 to 65.1 GW from 65.6 GW in 2024, and the Company's major export markets continue to face low demand; exports were 7.38% of turnover versus 7.85% last year.
- Fuel prices of imported gas used by most industries more than doubled and furnace oil prices rose by almost 50% on the West Asia war; the Company requested customers to accept a fuel surcharge covering part of the cost increase, did not curtail production and maintained full production, and states the rise in fuel cost has not impacted margins.
- GMB's revenue collapse is attributed to discontinuation of production in view of the sharp drop in demand after solar module manufacturing capacity shut down in the EU.
- The Company operates in a single primary business segment - the manufacture of flat glass - with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is presented only by geography (within India / outside India).
- Macro backdrop: IMF projects global growth of 3.1% in CY 2026 and 3.0% in CY 2027 with global inflation rising modestly to 4.4% in CY 2026; India's economy is estimated to have grown 7.6% in FY 2025-26, with Union Budget 2026-27 prioritising scaling manufacturing and deepening domestic value chains.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Borosil Renewables' expansion is concentrated at its single flagship solar-glass complex at Bharuch, Gujarat, a 100-acre site described as India's first and largest solar glass facility. The company's capacity has been built in steps: India's first solar glass line of 180 TPD in 2010, expansion to 450 TPD (equivalent to 2.8 GW/annum) in 2019, and a further 550 TPD addition in 2023 taking India capacity to a total of 1,000 TPD (equivalent to 6.5 GW per annum). The AR's combined-installed-capacity chart traces the same path across furnaces - Furnace 1 (India) 240 TPD, Furnace 2 (India) 210 TPD, Furnace 3 (India) 550 TPD, plus Furnace 1 (Europe) - from 180 TPD in CY18 to 1,000 TPD at July CY25, with 1,600 TPD shown as the Est CY26 position. The live project is the 600 TPD expansion designated SG 4&5, on which work was commenced during 2025. The company states the 600 TPD project entails an investment of Rs 950 crores and is targeted for completion by December 2026; once operational, total installed capacity will increase to 1,600 TPD, enabling it to support approximately 10.5 GW of solar module demand annually - described in the report as 'Combined Solar Glass Capacity Planned: 1600 TPD (~10.5 GW)'. The expansion is funded from a 2025 preferential issue of equity shares and warrants raising Rs 517.66 crores plus an additional Rs 371.49 crores, explicitly earmarked to expand production capacity by 60% at the Bharuch facility. Alongside glass capacity, the company invested in a second captive power plant of 16.5 MW of wind-solar hybrid generation under a group captive mechanism with high plant load factor; this plant achieved commercial operations in March 2026 (against an expectation of September 2025) and allows the company to meet about 75% of its power requirement from green energy while reducing power cost. On the product-mix side, the share of 2 mm glass production was raised to 75% with the stated aim of reaching 100% by Q4 FY 2026-27, and grid-printed glasses for bifacial modules were successfully introduced. Product/application widening also continues into greenhouse glass, anti-glare glass and Building-Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV). Working against this domestic build-out, the European footprint has been exited rather than expanded: step-down subsidiary GMB Glasmanufaktur Brandenburg GmbH discontinued production and filed for insolvency on July 04, 2025, and its holding company Geosphere Glassworks GmbH filed for insolvency on December 22, 2025, with the Board writing off the Rs 32,590.81 lakhs exposure; the Europe furnace consequently drops out of the combined capacity chart. Demand-side context cited for the expansion is India adding a record ~44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26 and cumulative solar installed capacity crossing 150 GW (150.26 GW as of March 31, 2026), against domestic solar glass production currently estimated at around 18 GW and expected to increase sharply to nearly 51 GW by FY 2026-27 as new capacities by existing and new entrants commence operations.

one-line thesis: A strong, price-and-protection-driven quarter: standalone sales +53% YoY to Rs 405.69 cr with EBITDA at 35% (Rs 142 cr) — a 4th straight quarter above 33% — as anti-dumping/CVD walls (China/Vietnam ADD since Dec-24; Malaysia CVD 9.71% extended 5 yrs) plus a domestic supply gap (local solar glass meets only ~25% of demand) hold import-parity pricing, while a fuel surcharge (Rs 9.50/sqm from 10-Mar-26) offsets the West-Asia-war energy spike. Plants ran at full 1,000 TPD; a new solar-wind hybrid captive lifted renewable power to 93% (~Rs 18 cr/yr savings). The core catalyst is the **600 TPD expansion (1,000→1,600 TPD, +60%)** — construction done by Dec-26, both furnaces (SG4/SG5) commissioned by Mar-27, revenue from FY28, adding ~Rs 80-85 cr incremental EBITDA/quarter. Management aspires to grow from ~Rs 2,500 cr to Rs 4,000 cr+ in 3-4 years and is deciding the next furnace/adjacency within ~6 months. Note the reported PAT optics: Q4FY26's Rs 169 cr carried a Rs 75 cr one-off tax write-back (German write-off), so the QoQ "profit halving" to ~Rs 87 cr is an artifact, not operational decay.

> Optics to watch: (1) QoQ PAT "drop" to ~Rs 87 cr is purely the Rs 75 cr Q4 tax write-back reversing out — operations are flat-to-up QoQ (EBITDA Rs 144.61→Rs 142 cr). (2) The Rs 160 realization is inflated by the Rs 9.50 fuel surcharge, which will compress (and is already being trimmed) as fuel costs ease — neutral to profit since costs fall in tandem.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **600 TPD expansion (1,000→1,600 TPD, +60% capacity):** construction complete by **Dec-26**, both furnaces (SG4 + SG5, ~1-month gap) commissioned **by Mar-27 (Q4 FY27)**; model revenue from **1-Apr-27 / FY28** (internal target 1-Mar; management advises conservative FY28). → **sales +60%; incremental EBITDA ~Rs 80-85 cr per quarter** at current prices.
- **Rooftop solar (solar-kit) revenue: ~Rs 36 cr for FY27** (Q1 did ~Rs 1.3 cr); single-digit EBITDA (trading, not 30-35% manufacturing).
- **Revenue aspiration: ~Rs 2,500 cr → Rs 4,000 cr+ in 3-4 years** (post-Mar-27), via an additional solar-glass furnace and/or an adjacent glass field.
- **Next-round expansion decision (furnace 600 vs 1,200 TPD, or adjacency) in ~5-6 months** (H2 FY27).
- **EBITDA margin higher YoY in FY27** — full-price realization across the whole year (vs price ramp-up in H1 FY26 post-ADD).
- **Full-year effective tax rate ~25.2%.**
- **Fuel surcharge (Rs 9.50) to compress / be passed back** as fuel costs ease (profit-neutral — cost falls too).
- **No equity raise foreseen near-term**; current expansion fully funded; next round funded by cash generation (+ some debt if project large).
order book & pipeline: - No formal order book (commodity-adjacent manufacturer). Demand context: 62 GW (DC) module installs FY26; module capacity now 203 GW (vs 11 GW 5 yrs ago). 62 GW needs ~11,000 TPD solar glass vs domestic ~2,600 TPD (~18 GW) today → rising to ~7,700 TPD (~51 GW) by Mar-27, **still a supply gap** (domestic covers ~25% of demand). Customer concentration: **top 10 = 65-68% of volume**; customers increasingly large (10-15 players at 5-15 GW). Incremental 600 TPD earmarked flexibly for existing large accounts scale-up + re-adding customers previously un-serviced due to "paucity of material." US exports very small today (niche apps), a potential future market.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Solar glass (core):** full-capacity 1,000 TPD; +8% volume, +53% value (price-led). Import-parity pricing under ADD/CVD protection.
- **Rooftop solar-kit (new):** module+inverter+battery on-grid residential system (2-3 states first, then C&I); brand-leverage play; trading economics (single-digit EBITDA); ~Rs 36 cr FY27 target.
- **Overseas (Germany — Geosphere / GMB):** investment written off (Rs 325 cr); insolvent; ~nil revenue — the historic EBITDA drag (-Rs 23 cr YoY quarter) is essentially gone.
- **Captive power:** solar-wind hybrid (Mar-26) → 93% renewable power, ~Rs 18 cr/yr savings.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **600 TPD brownfield** (the committed near-term engine: +60% sales/EBITDA from FY28).
- **Next furnace (600/1,200 TPD) or glass adjacency** — decision in ~6 months; path to Rs 4,000 cr+.
- **Rooftop solar-kit** — small now, but "much bigger opportunity in turnover" if volumes scale.
- **US market** — future optionality, negligible today.
- **Policy tailwinds:** ALMM 2 (cells, 1-Jun-26), ALMM 3 (ingot/wafer, from 28-Jun) deepen the domestic PV chain and pull solar-glass demand; EV/data-center/green-hydrogen as incremental demand drivers.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Only listed domestic solar-glass pure-play at scale** into a structural supply gap (domestic ~25% of demand) — import-parity pricing power evidenced by +53% value on +8% volume.
- **Trade-remedy moat:** ADD on China/Vietnam (Dec-24) + Malaysia CVD 9.71% (extended 5 yrs to 2031) cap import competition; reference price = landed import parity.
- **Cost/ESG edge:** 93% renewable captive power (~Rs 18 cr/yr savings) — a durable unit-cost advantage vs a fuel-exposed process.
- Management explicitly: "we don't foresee any kind of challenge on the pricing" even as domestic capacity rises to 7,700 TPD, because much of new capacity is captive and demand stays ~75% short.
margins & cost dynamics:
- EBITDA 35% (>33% for 4 straight quarters); gross margin ~78% (RM ~23-24%); no material RM/price volatility expected → EBITDA margin set to rise YoY in FY27 on full-year full-price realization (H1 FY26 was still ramping post-ADD).
- Fuel surcharge (Rs 9.50) offsets war-driven gas/oil spike; already being trimmed as fuel eases (profit-neutral pass-through, committed to customers).
- Renewable captive power (93%) structurally lowers energy cost.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **600 TPD (SG4/SG5):** fully funded, layout frozen, building under construction; done Dec-26, commissioned by Mar-27, revenue FY28. Watch: 1-2 month furnace stabilization → management models revenue only from 1-Apr (conservative).
- **SG1/SG2 furnace rebuild** (every 6-7 yrs; refractories at 1,600 C): **~90-day shutdown (75 rebuild + 15 restart) with quantum volume loss**, timing uncertain — likely **Q4 FY27 or Q1/Q2 FY28**, probably after SG4/SG5 are live. Q1 saw only a minor 4-day SG1 tile patch (~Rs 3 cr value). This is the key FY28 volume swing to model.
- Next-round furnace = separate new project/building (600 or 1,200 TPD, TBD in ~6 months).
capital allocation:
- Current expansion fully funded; no near-term equity raise. Next round funded by cash generation post-Mar-27 (+ some debt only if project large).
- German subsidiary investment written off (Rs 325 cr) — capital-loss recognized, overseas drag cleaned up; tax shield realized.
- Reinvesting in capacity (glass) + a small brand-extension bet (rooftop kit); dividend/buyback not discussed.
risks & watch-items:
- **Fuel/energy volatility (West Asia war):** oil swinging $72-85; surcharge cushions but a policy/logistics shock could hit cost; govt lifting supply curbs should restore full contracted volumes.
- **SG1/SG2 rebuild volume loss** (~90 days) in FY28 window — dents the 1,600 TPD run-rate.
- **Module-industry over-capacity & consolidation** (203 GW vs demand; Mono-PERC obsolescence; cell-short module makers may "not continue") → some customer churn/credit risk; Borosil will re-pick customers.
- **Domestic solar-glass capacity ramp** (2,600→7,700 TPD by Mar-27) — management argues captive share + supply gap keep pricing firm, but a demand air-pocket could pressure price.
- **Policy dependence:** business is "policy-driven" (ADD/CVD, PLI, ALMM) — reversal/dilution is a tail risk.
- **Rooftop-kit execution:** nascent, low-margin trading, brand-extension risk.
management quality / tone: - Ashok Jain fielded nearly every question with specificity — corrected an analyst's confused PAT comparison (patiently walking through the Rs 75 cr tax write-back), quantified surcharge (Rs 9.50), savings (Rs 18 cr/yr), incremental EBITDA (Rs 80-85 cr/qtr), and was candid on furnace-rebuild volume loss (won't sandbag). Refused to over-guide ("not appropriate to give guidance") yet gave a clear 3-4 yr Rs 4,000 cr aspiration and a 6-month decision clock. Declined to comment on "strategic investment" press articles (appropriately). Explained promoter time-split across 3 listed cos (Chairman P.K. Kheruka fully on Renewables). Tone: confident, transparent, policy-literate.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The QoQ "profit halved" scare is a pure accounting artifact: Q4FY26 PAT Rs 169 cr embedded a Rs 75 cr tax write-back tied to the German write-off; strip it and Q1 operations (EBITDA Rs 142 cr vs Rs 144.61 cr) are essentially flat QoQ and up 53% YoY.
- Realization quality: the headline Rs 160/sqm is Rs 9.50 fuel-surcharge-inflated and will compress as fuel eases — so don't extrapolate Rs 160; the "clean" price is ~Rs 150 and margin is protected because cost falls alongside the surcharge.
- The real moat is regulatory + structural scarcity, not just cost: ADD/CVD walls + a domestic supply gap (25% self-sufficiency) give import-parity pricing power that a +53%-value-on-+8%-volume quarter makes visible.
- The 600 TPD brownfield is high-confidence and near (Mar-27), but the FY28 P&L has an offsetting hidden variable — the SG1/SG2 ~90-day rebuild — so gross FY28 volume uplift will be less than the +60% nameplate suggests.
- German overseas chapter is closed (write-off done, ~nil revenue, drag removed) — consolidated now cleanly reflects the profitable India business; a quiet positive for reported consol EBITDA (-Rs 23 cr YoY quarter drag → -Rs 0.84 cr).

themes.title: Renewable IPP / FDRE firm-power & storage
themes.need: DISCOMs mandating firm/round-the-clock RE make BESS + pumped-hydro the bid differentiator, and in Q1FY27 storage demand ran ahead of supply. ADANIGREEN has 3.5 GWh of BESS installed (+1.9 GWh at Khavda this quarter), targets 10+ GWh this fiscal and 50 GWh by FY30 on a thumb-rule INR 25-30 lakh of EBITDA per MWh against ~INR 1.5cr/MWh of capex, and has contracted essentially all merchant/C&I capacity to sibling AESL on 25-year (solar/wind) and 15-year (battery) fixed-price PPAs targeting ~15-16% IRR - a pivot from merchant builder to fixed-return contracted IPP, with evacuation (not panels) named as the binding constraint. JSWENERGY added 873 MW in Q1 and ~1.1 GW since April - 36% of its 3 GW FY27 target already banked, Tidong Hydro commissioned four months early - and raised INR 10,150cr, taking net leverage 5.2x to 4.95x. On the equipment side SERVOTECH said its BESS pack capacity is fully booked ('we are not able to meet the demand') and committed to 2x capacity in 6 months, 3x by 21-Mar-2027 and 10x within 2 years. ACMESOLAR/KPIGREEN/SUZLON/INOXWIND attach storage to solar/wind; NTPC/NHPC/SJVN/TATAPOWER drive pumped-hydro and utility-scale storage.
themes.driver: BESS capacity commissioning against demand two independent managements (ADANIGREEN, SERVOTECH) say already exceeds supply; FDRE/peak-power tender awards; merchant DAM prices (JSWENERGY: INR 4.40 -> INR 5.10/unit, +16%) on +8.5% Q1 power demand.
